learning_objectives: Calculate moment of inertia for discrete point masses and continuous bodies using integration and the parallel/perpendicular axis theorems.
Formulate rotational equations of motion tau = I alpha and apply work-energy principles to fixed axis rotation.
Determine the angular momentum of particles and rigid bodies about fixed reference points and instantaneous axes of rotation.
Apply the principle of conservation of angular momentum to isolated systems with time-varying moments of inertia.
Analyze pure rolling kinematics and dynamics on horizontal and inclined surfaces under static friction constraints.

formula_sequence.title: Parallel Axis Theorem

variables.I: Moment of inertia about arbitrary parallel axis
variables.I_{\\text{cm}}: Moment of inertia about parallel axis through center of mass

assumptions: Rigid body with constant mass distribution
conditions_of_validity: One axis must pass strictly through the center of mass
common_misuse_cases: Applying parallel axis theorem between two arbitrary parallel axes neither of which passes through the center of mass

formula_sequence.title: Fixed Axis Rotational Dynamics

variables.\\tau_{\\text{net, ext}}: Net external torque about fixed rotation axis
variables.I: Moment of inertia about rotation axis

assumptions: Fixed rotation axis or axis passing through CM in principal orientation
conditions_of_validity: Valid about a fixed inertial axis or about the center of mass even if accelerating
common_misuse_cases: Applying tau = I alpha about an arbitrary accelerating point other than the center of mass

formula_sequence.title: Angular Momentum of a Particle

variables.\\vec{L}_O: Angular momentum vector about point O
variables.\\vec{r}: Position vector of particle relative to O

assumptions: Reference point O is an inertial point or specified origin
conditions_of_validity: Valid for any particle trajectory in 3D Euclidean space
common_misuse_cases: Assuming angular momentum is zero for a particle moving in a straight line; it is non-zero about any origin not on the trajectory line

formula_sequence.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum About Fixed Axis

variables.I_i: Initial moment of inertia about axis
variables.I_f: Final moment of inertia about axis

assumptions: System rotates about a fixed axis
Mass redistribution does not introduce external torque along axis
conditions_of_validity: Net external torque component along the axis of rotation must be zero (tau_ext,z = 0)
common_misuse_cases: Assuming conservation of kinetic energy when moment of inertia changes due to internal work, e.g. crawling insect or pulling string

misconception_sequence.statement: A particle moving along a straight line at constant velocity has zero angular momentum.
misconception_sequence.explanation: Angular momentum is defined as L = r x p. For straight-line motion, L = m v r_perp, where r_perp is the impact parameter (perpendicular distance from origin to line of motion). As long as the line of motion does not pass through the reference point O, r_perp is non-zero, and L is constant and non-zero.
misconception_sequence.trap_mechanism: Exam questions ask about angular momentum of a freely falling body or particle in straight line about an offset point, expecting students to equate linear motion with zero rotational quantities.
trigger_conditions: Particle moving in vertical free fall near earth
Origin chosen on the ground but not directly beneath the release point

misconception_sequence.statement: When a system conserves angular momentum under internal reconfiguration, mechanical energy is also conserved.
misconception_sequence.explanation: Internal forces that alter mass distribution (such as an insect walking radially on a rotating disc or an ice skater pulling in their arms) do work. Consequently, rotational kinetic energy K = L^2 / (2 I) varies inversely with I. Energy is NOT conserved, even though angular momentum is strictly conserved because internal forces exert zero net external torque.
misconception_sequence.trap_mechanism: Questions test whether students attempt to equate initial and final kinetic energies when mass distribution changes, leading to incorrect velocity calculations.
trigger_conditions: Insect crawling on rotating turntable or disc
Radial movement of sliding collar on rotating rod

worked_example_sequence.problem_statement: A uniform circular disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rotating horizontally about a frictionless vertical axle passing through its center with angular velocity $\omega_0$. A small insect of mass $m$ is initially at the center of the disc. The insect crawls slowly along a radial line towards the rim of the disc until it reaches the edge. (a) Determine the angular velocity $\omega(r)$ of the disc as a function of the insect's radial distance $r$ from the center. (b) Find the ratio of the final rotational kinetic energy to the initial rotational kinetic energy when the insect reaches $r = R$.

known_quantities.r: Radial position of insect from center

worked_example_sequence.target_quantity: Angular velocity omega(r) and kinetic energy ratio K_f / K_i
governing_principles: Conservation of Angular Momentum: sum tau_ext,z = 0 implies L_z = constant
worked_example_sequence.solution_strategy: Identify that no external torque acts about the vertical rotation axis. Apply conservation of angular momentum L_i = L_f to find omega as a function of r. Then express rotational kinetic energy K = (1/2) I omega^2 = L^2 / (2 I) to find the energy ratio directly.
step_by_step_derivation: Step 1: Compute initial moment of inertia I_i when insect is at r = 0: I_i = I_disc + m(0)^2 = (1/2) M R^2.
Step 2: Compute moment of inertia I(r) when insect is at radial distance r: I(r) = (1/2) M R^2 + m r^2.

Step 3: Conserve angular momentum about the vertical axle: L = I_i omega_0 = I(r) omega(r). Thus, omega(r) = (I_i / I(r)) omega_0 = ((1/2) M R^2 / ((1/2) M R^2 + m r^2)) omega_0 = (M R^2 / (M R^2 + 2 m r^2)) omega_0.
Step 4: At the rim r = R, I_f = (1/2) M R^2 + m R^2 = ((M + 2m) / 2) R^2. The final angular velocity is omega_f = (M / (M + 2m)) omega_0.
Step 5: The rotational kinetic energy is K = L^2 / (2 I). Since L is constant, K_f / K_i = I_i / I_f = ((1/2) M R^2) / (((M + 2m)/2) R^2) = M / (M + 2m).
sanity_checks: Limiting case m -> 0: omega(r) -> omega_0 and K_f/K_i -> 1 as expected.
Physical consistency: As insect moves outwards, I increases so omega decreases and rotational kinetic energy decreases because insect does negative work resisting centrifugal effects.

revision_checklist: Moment of Inertia formulas for standard geometric bodies (rod, ring, disc, sphere, cylinder).
Parallel Axis Theorem: I = I_cm + M d^2 (must pass strictly through CM).
Perpendicular Axis Theorem: I_z = I_x + I_y (planar bodies only).
Torque: tau = r x F, and rotational dynamics tau_ext = I alpha (valid about fixed axis or CM).
Angular Momentum of a particle: L = r x p = m v r_perp.
Angular Momentum of a rigid body: L = I omega.
Conservation of Angular Momentum: dL/dt = tau_ext = 0 implies L_i = L_f.
Work done in rotation: W = int tau d theta, Kinetic energy K = (1/2) I omega^2.
Pure rolling condition: v_cm = R omega, a_cm = R alpha (point of contact instantaneously at rest).
